blocks.content: Here is a number that should change how you write code: you will read it about ten times more often than you write it.
Every bug fix, every new feature, every code review starts with someone reading what is already there. If that code is hard to follow, every one of those moments gets slower and more painful.
Readable code is not about looking pretty. It is about letting the next person, often future you, understand it quickly and change it safely.
1. Readability Beats Cleverness
It is tempting to feel proud of a tight, clever one liner. But clever code is usually write once and confuse forever. The reader has to decode it before they can trust it.
Code is read far more often than it is written. Optimise for the reader, not for your own typing.
2. Names That Explain Themselves
The fastest way to make code readable is to name things well. A good name answers the reader question before they even ask it.
You should rarely need a comment to explain what a variable holds when its name already says so. We go deep on this in the Naming Conventions lesson.
3. Keep Functions Small and Focused
A function you can read top to bottom without scrolling, one that does exactly a single thing, is a function you can trust. Long functions hide bugs in their middle.
["One function, one job","A name that fully describes that single job","Few arguments, ideally three or fewer","No surprises hidden inside"]
items: A name that fully describes that single job
Few arguments, ideally three or fewer

blocks.content: If you find yourself adding a comment like "now we validate the input" above a block, that block usually wants to become its own well named function.
4. Flatten the Nesting
Deeply nested code is one of the biggest readability killers. Every extra level of indentation is another condition the reader has to hold in their head at once.
The cure is the guard clause: handle the edge cases early and return, so the main logic stays at the left margin where it is easy to see.
Every level of indentation is a tax on the reader. Pay it back with early returns.
5. Be Consistent
Consistency lets a reader predict your code. When the same idea always looks the same way, their brain stops spending energy on the shape and focuses on the meaning.

["Use one naming style across the whole codebase","Order things the same way: fields, then constructor, then methods","Format with a shared tool so nobody argues about spaces","Solve similar problems with similar patterns"]
items: Use one naming style across the whole codebase
Order things the same way: fields, then constructor, then methods
Format with a shared tool so nobody argues about spaces
Solve similar problems with similar patterns

blocks.content: A consistent codebase that is slightly imperfect is far easier to read than a perfect file surrounded by chaos.
6. Let the Code Speak
The best readable code barely needs explaining. Before adding a comment, ask whether a better name or a small extracted function would remove the need for it entirely.

codes.python:
# needs a comment to be understood
# check if the user can access the report
if u.role == 2 and u.active and not u.banned:
    ...

# explains itself, no comment needed
if user.can_view_reports():
    ...

blocks.content: We cover exactly where that balance sits in the Commenting Best Practices lesson.
10. Common Questions
Is readable code slower to write? A little, at first. But you make that time back many times over the moment you, or anyone else, has to read or change it. Slow to write, fast to live with.

What if the clever version is faster? Measure first. Most clever tricks save nothing meaningful. When performance truly matters, keep the fast code but add a short comment explaining why it looks the way it does.
How small should a function really be? Small enough that its name fully describes it and you can read it without scrolling. If you need the word "and" to name it, it is doing too much.
Does readability matter in throwaway scripts? Less so. The rule scales with how long the code lives and how many people touch it. For code that ships and stays, readability is not optional.
Readable code is a gift to your future self and your teammates. Write for the human who reads it next, and the machine will run it just the same.
7. Naming Variables, Methods, and Classes With Precision
blocks.text: 7. Naming Variables, Methods, and Classes With Precision

blocks.content: Section 2 showed how a good variable name saves a comment. That same discipline has to extend to every identifier in your code: methods, classes, parameters, even boolean flags. Vague names spread confusion faster than almost any other habit in a codebase.
Variables Hold Data, So Name the Data
blocks.text: Variables Hold Data, So Name the Data

blocks.content: A variable name should tell the reader what is stored, not just its type. "list", "data", "temp", and "obj" are all technically valid names, and all equally useless. "pendingOrders", "rawResponseBody", and "retryCount" tell the reader something the type alone never could.
Methods Perform Actions, So Name the Action
blocks.text: Methods Perform Actions, So Name the Action

blocks.content: A method name should read like a sentence when combined with its arguments. "cart.applyDiscount(code)" reads naturally, while "cart.discount(code)" leaves the reader guessing whether this reads a discount or applies one. Favor a verb at the front, calculate, validate, build, fetch, so the call site tells its own story.
Classes Represent One Concept, So Name the Concept
blocks.text: Classes Represent One Concept, So Name the Concept

blocks.content: A class name should be a noun that describes what the object is, not what it does technically. "InvoiceGenerator" is fine, but "Manager", "Handler", and "Processor" attached to almost anything are a sign the class has no clear identity of its own. If you cannot describe a class in one plain sentence, the name is probably too vague, or the class is doing too much.
Cut the Abbreviations and the Generic Placeholders
blocks.text: Cut the Abbreviations and the Generic Placeholders

blocks.content: Abbreviations save the writer a few keystrokes and cost the reader far more time decoding them. "usrCnt", "calcTtl", and "mgrRef" all force a small mental puzzle before they can be understood. Spell the word out instead: "userCount", "calculateTotal", "managerReference". Modern editors autocomplete the rest, so brevity buys nothing.

codes.python:
# before: cryptic and generic
def proc(u, d):
    f = d["p"] * (1 - d["disc"])
    r = f * 0.9 if f > 100 else f
    u["bal"] -= r
    return r

# after: names explain themselves
def charge_user_for_order(user, order_details):
    price_after_discount = order_details["price"] * (1 - order_details["discount"])
    final_price = price_after_discount * 0.9 if price_after_discount > 100 else price_after_discount

    user["balance"] -= final_price
    return final_price

blocks.content: Nothing about the logic changed between the two versions. Only the names did, yet the after version can be reviewed in seconds while the before version needs a whiteboard and a guess.

["Prefer a full word over an abbreviation, \"quantity\" over \"qty\"","Name booleans as questions, such as \"isActive\", \"hasPermission\", \"canEdit\"","Avoid noise words that add length without meaning, such as \"data\", \"info\", \"manager\", \"helper\"","Keep a name length proportional to its scope, short names for a tiny loop, fuller names for anything longer lived","Use the same word for the same concept everywhere, do not alternate between \"fetch\", \"get\", and \"retrieve\" for identical operations","Never encode the type in the name, let the type system carry that job"]
items: Prefer a full word over an abbreviation, "quantity" over "qty"
Name booleans as questions, such as "isActive", "hasPermission", "canEdit"
Avoid noise words that add length without meaning, such as "data", "info", "manager", "helper"
Keep a name length proportional to its scope, short names for a tiny loop, fuller names for anything longer lived
Use the same word for the same concept everywhere, do not alternate between "fetch", "get", and "retrieve" for identical operations
Never encode the type in the name, let the type system carry that job

blocks.content: A codebase where every name is precise reads almost like documentation. That is the goal: code so clear that comments become optional, not code you have to memorize.
8. Formatting and Structure a Reader Can Predict
blocks.text: 8. Formatting and Structure a Reader Can Predict

blocks.content: Naming and small functions make code easy to think about. Layout makes it easy to scan. When files, classes, and blocks always follow the same shape, a reader learns where to look before they even start reading the logic.
Keep a Standard Order Inside a Class
blocks.text: Keep a Standard Order Inside a Class

blocks.content: Pick one order for members, for example constants, then fields, then constructor, then public methods, then private helpers, and use it in every class. A reader who knows the convention can jump straight to the constructor without scanning the whole file.
Use Blank Lines as Punctuation

A blank line groups related statements the way a paragraph break groups related sentences. Leave one between a block that sets up some state and the block that uses it. Do not scatter blank lines randomly, every one should mark a real shift in the flow, not just relieve visual density.
Let a Formatter Own the Small Decisions
blocks.text: Let a Formatter Own the Small Decisions

blocks.content: Spacing, indentation width, brace placement, none of these decisions matter much on their own, but disagreeing about them wastes review time and clutters diffs with noise. Adopt one automatic formatter for the project and let it settle every argument, so the energy saved goes into reviewing logic instead of arguing about tabs.

["Run an automatic formatter on save so style never becomes a discussion","Keep line length short enough to read without horizontal scrolling","Group related fields and methods together instead of scattering them by when they were added","Give similar problems the same shape, so two methods that validate two different forms use the same order of checks and the same naming pattern for the result"]
items: Run an automatic formatter on save so style never becomes a discussion
Keep line length short enough to read without horizontal scrolling
Group related fields and methods together instead of scattering them by when they were added
Give similar problems the same shape, so two methods that validate two different forms use the same order of checks and the same naming pattern for the result

blocks.content: None of these rules are about beauty. They are about removing the small frictions that slow a reader down before they even reach the part that matters.
9. A Worked Refactor: From Dense to Readable
blocks.text: 9. A Worked Refactor: From Dense to Readable

blocks.content: The best way to see all of this together is to refactor one real method. Below is a single function that validates an order, applies a discount, computes shipping, and logs the result, all crammed into one block with no clear boundary between the steps.
One Method, Four Responsibilities

Read through the before version first and notice how many different jobs "proc" is doing, and how little its name or its variable names tell you about any of them. Then compare it with the after version, where each responsibility has moved into its own well named function.

The extraction did not change what the code computes. It changed how much a reader has to hold in their head at once. The top level function now reads like a table of contents: calculate the subtotal, apply the coupon, calculate shipping, validate, log, return.
Why This Version Wins

Each extracted function can be tested on its own, without setting up an entire order. A future change, such as adding a new coupon code, now touches only "applyCoupon" instead of risking a typo somewhere inside a nineteen line block. And a reviewer scanning the diff for that change sees exactly one small function change, not a wall of unrelated logic.

This is the whole discipline in miniature: give every piece a name that describes its one job, and the structure of the code starts to explain itself.
